title: Why Translations Differ
summary: Word-for-word and thought-for-thought, the choices every translator faces, the history of the English Bible from Bede to the present, and how to read small capitals, brackets, italics, and footnotes.

sections.h: Every translation is a set of decisions
sections.body:
Anyone who has learned a second language knows that words do not match one for one. A Hebrew or Greek word may have a range of meaning that no single English word covers; a construction natural in one language is clumsy or meaningless in another; an idiom that is vivid in the original may be nonsense when rendered literally. A translator must decide, at every line, how much of the original's form to keep and how much to reshape so that the meaning comes through.

The Bible offers examples on every page. When God proclaims his name to Moses, he calls himself “slow to anger” (Exodus 34:6); the Hebrew phrase, ‘erek appayim, means literally ‘long of nostrils’, since in Hebrew idiom anger shows in the flaring and heat of the nose. No English Bible prints the literal wording, because it would mislead. Genesis 4:1 says in Hebrew that Adam ‘knew’ his wife, which the King James Version kept and which the BSB renders “Adam had relations with his wife Eve”. Paul's word sarx means ‘flesh’, but in his letters it often means human nature in its weakness and rebellion against God; the NIV of 1984 rendered it ‘sinful nature’ in many places, and the NIV of 2011 returned to ‘flesh’ with notes, judging that the interpretation had become too narrow.

Some decisions are theological. Paul's Greek phrase pistis Christou in Galatians 2:16 and several other places can be read as ‘faith in Christ’ (Christ as the object of faith) or ‘the faithfulness of Christ’ (Christ as the one who is faithful). Richard Hays, in The Faith of Jesus Christ (1983), argued for the second; James D. G. Dunn and many others defended the first. Most translations, including the BSB, read ‘faith in Christ’, and several now give the other reading in a footnote. Romans 12:1 calls the offering of our bodies a logikē latreia, which the KJV renders ‘reasonable service’, the ESV ‘spiritual worship’, the NIV ‘true and proper worship’, and the BSB “spiritual service of worship”. Each captures part of a phrase that means worship fitting for rational creatures and fitting for the new life of the Spirit.

No translation escapes interpretation. That is not a defect in translation; it is what translation is. The practical lesson for a reader is to use more than one translation, and to notice where they differ, since differences usually mark the places where the original is dense, ambiguous, or disputed.

Translations are usually placed on a spectrum. At one end are formal-equivalence translations, sometimes called essentially literal or word-for-word, which try to keep the words, word order, and grammatical structures of the original wherever English allows, and to render a given Hebrew or Greek word consistently. The King James Version, the New American Standard Bible, the English Standard Version, and the Legacy Standard Bible stand here. Their strength is transparency: the reader can see repeated words, metaphors, and ambiguities that the original leaves open. Their weakness is that English shaped closely to Hebrew or Greek can be stiff, and literal wording can obscure meaning when an idiom does not carry over.

At the other end are functional-equivalence translations, sometimes called thought-for-thought or dynamic equivalence. The terms come from Eugene Nida of the American Bible Society, who in Toward a Science of Translating (1964) described ‘dynamic equivalence’ as producing in modern readers the response the original produced in its first readers; Nida and Jan de Waard later preferred the term functional equivalence (From One Language to Another, 1986). The Good News Translation, the Contemporary English Version, and the New Living Translation stand toward this end. Their strength is clarity and naturalness; they are often the best Bibles for a first reading, for children, and for readers of English as a second language. Their weakness is that the translator's interpretation is built into the text, and features of the original that a reader might want to notice are smoothed away.

Many translations sit in between, aiming at what the Christian Standard Bible calls optimal equivalence: literal where literal wording is clear, freer where it is not. The New International Version, the Christian Standard Bible, the NET Bible, and the Berean Standard Bible used in this Study Bible belong here, each leaning slightly one way or the other. Beyond the functional end lie paraphrases, which restate the text freely in contemporary idiom: Kenneth Taylor's Living Bible (1971) and Eugene Peterson's The Message (completed 2002). Paraphrases can be vivid companions but are not meant as study texts.

Critics of each approach make serious points. Defenders of formal equivalence, such as Leland Ryken (The Word of God in English, 2002), argue that the words of Scripture are inspired, not only its ideas, and that translators should leave interpretation to readers. Defenders of functional equivalence, such as Gordon Fee and Mark Strauss (How to Choose a Translation for All Its Worth, 2007), reply that meaning is carried by whole phrases and sentences, not single words, and that a stiff translation can distort meaning as surely as a loose one. Both sides agree that the best practice is to read across the spectrum.

sections.body:
Translations differ not only in how they translate but in what they translate. For the Old Testament, nearly all English Bibles translate the Masoretic Text, the standard Hebrew text preserved by medieval Jewish scholars (see How We Got the Old Testament), and depart from it only occasionally where the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, or another ancient witness seems to preserve a better reading. Translations differ in how often they do this: the NRSV and NRSVue do it more readily, the NASB and KJV rarely. Some Orthodox translations, such as the Old Testament of the Orthodox Study Bible (2008), translate the Septuagint instead, because it is the Old Testament of the Orthodox church.

For the New Testament, the main dividing line is between translations based on the Textus Receptus, the Greek text printed from Erasmus in 1516 to the Elzevirs in 1633, and those based on modern critical editions such as Nestle-Aland (see How We Got the New Testament). The KJV and NKJV follow the Textus Receptus; almost every other modern translation follows a critical text. This is why passages such as 1 John 5:7-8, Acts 8:37, and Matthew 6:13's closing doxology appear in the KJV and not in most modern Bibles, and why readers who move from the KJV to a modern Bible find some verse numbers apparently missing. The BSB translates the Hebrew Masoretic Text, following the Leningrad Codex, and a modern critical Greek text, and footnotes significant differences among the ancient witnesses.

Neither choice is a conspiracy. Defenders of the Textus Receptus and of the Byzantine majority text argue that the text the church used for most of its history deserves priority; defenders of the critical text argue that the earliest manuscripts, unknown or unused in the sixteenth century, bring us closer to what the apostles wrote. The differences are real but concern a small portion of the text, and good modern Bibles print the alternatives in their notes.

sections.h: Contested choices: gender, names, and holy words
sections.body:
Some translation debates are fierce because they touch contested questions in church and culture. The most prominent in recent decades concerns gender language. Greek adelphoi, literally ‘brothers’, was used by Paul for whole congregations of men and women; Hebrew and Greek words for ‘man’ often mean ‘person’ or ‘human being’; and generic ‘he’ has fallen out of common English. The NRSV (1989) rendered adelphoi as ‘brothers and sisters’ and generic ‘man’ with inclusive terms throughout; the NIV Inclusive Language Edition in Britain (1996) and Today's New International Version (2002 and 2005) did the same for the NIV, and the NIV of 2011 kept most of those choices. Critics, including Vern Poythress and Wayne Grudem (The Gender-Neutral Bible Controversy, 2000), argued that these changes altered meaning, and a group convened in 1997 issued the Colorado Springs Guidelines for gender language. D. A. Carson (The Inclusive Language Debate, 1998) urged realism on both sides, arguing that some inclusive renderings are accurate and some are not, and that English usage genuinely has changed. The ESV and CSB generally keep ‘brothers’ with a footnote explaining that the term can include women; the BSB also keeps “brothers” (for example, Romans 12:1). Each approach intends accuracy; they disagree about what English readers will actually hear.

Other decisions concern holy words. How to render the divine name YHWH is discussed below. Many older Bibles and some modern ones, including the BSB, capitalize pronouns referring to God (He, His, You); others do not, reasoning that Hebrew and Greek have no capital letters and that deciding which pronouns refer to God is sometimes an interpretation (as in some psalms applied to the Messiah). Names are transliterated differently: Hebrew yeshua‘ comes into Greek as Iēsous and English as Jesus, and the same Greek name is Joshua in Hebrews 4:8. Terms such as ‘Christ’ (Greek christos, ‘anointed one’, translating Hebrew mashiach, ‘Messiah’) can be translated or kept as titles. Some translations render Greek Ioudaioi in John's Gospel as ‘the Jewish leaders’ where the context points to the authorities, to avoid suggesting that John condemns the Jewish people as a whole; others keep ‘the Jews’ and explain it in notes. None of these choices is neutral, and a good translation explains its choices in its preface.

sections.h: The English Bible, from Bede to the King James
sections.body:
Parts of the Bible were rendered into Old English well before the Norman Conquest. According to a letter of his pupil Cuthbert, the scholar Bede was translating the Gospel of John into English on his deathbed in 735, and in the tenth century a priest named Aldred added an Old English word-by-word gloss between the lines of the Latin Lindisfarne Gospels. The first complete English Bible was the work of followers of the Oxford theologian John Wycliffe in the 1380s, translated from the Latin Vulgate in an early and then a revised, more idiomatic version. Because Wycliffe's followers, the Lollards, were judged heretical, the Constitutions of Archbishop Thomas Arundel (1409) forbade anyone to translate Scripture into English, or read such a translation, without episcopal approval. Wycliffite Bibles were still copied by hand in large numbers.

The printed English Bible begins with William Tyndale, an Oxford-trained scholar who could not obtain permission to translate in England and went to Germany. His New Testament, translated from Erasmus's Greek, was printed at Worms in 1526 and smuggled into England, where copies were burned. He went on to translate the Pentateuch (1530) and other Old Testament books from Hebrew. He was arrested in Antwerp, and on 6 October 1536 he was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde near Brussels. Tyndale's plain, rhythmic English shaped every English Bible after him. A study by Jon Nielson and Royal Skousen (1998) estimated that about 83 to 84 percent of the King James New Testament and about 76 percent of the Old Testament books Tyndale translated keep his wording.

The years that followed produced a rapid series of Bibles. Miles Coverdale published the first complete printed English Bible in 1535, using Tyndale where available and German and Latin versions elsewhere. Matthew's Bible (1537), edited by John Rogers under a pseudonym, gathered all of Tyndale's work; the Great Bible (1539), revised by Coverdale at the command of Thomas Cromwell, was the first English Bible authorized for reading in churches. Under Mary I, Protestant exiles in Geneva produced the Geneva Bible (1560), with verse numbers, readable roman type, maps, and extensive notes, many of them Calvinist in theology; it was the Bible of Shakespeare, John Bunyan, and the Pilgrims. The bishops of the Church of England answered with the Bishops' Bible (1568). English Catholics in exile produced the Douay-Rheims version from the Vulgate, New Testament at Rheims (1582) and Old Testament at Douai (1609 to 1610), revised in the eighteenth century by Bishop Richard Challoner.

At the Hampton Court Conference of January 1604 the Puritan leader John Reynolds proposed a new translation, and King James I took it up, partly because he disliked the Geneva notes. About fifty scholars (forty-seven names survive) worked in six companies at Westminster, Oxford, and Cambridge, instructed to revise the Bishops' Bible and to consult Tyndale, Coverdale, Matthew, the Great Bible, and Geneva. The result, printed by Robert Barker in 1611, was slow to displace the Geneva Bible but became for three centuries the English Bible. The text most people read today as the KJV is Benjamin Blayney's Oxford revision of 1769, which standardized spelling and punctuation and corrected many printing errors.

sections.h: From the Revised Version to the present
sections.body:
By the nineteenth century, the discovery of older manuscripts and the changes in English itself led to calls for revision. The Revised Version (New Testament 1881, Old Testament 1885) was produced by British scholars, with an American counterpart, the American Standard Version (1901). They followed the new critical Greek text of Westcott and Hort's era and were very literal. The Revised Standard Version (New Testament 1946, Old Testament 1952), sponsored by the National Council of Churches in the United States, updated the ASV in more modern English; some conservatives objected to particular renderings, notably ‘young woman’ in Isaiah 7:14, and this contributed to the creation of evangelical translations. The New American Standard Bible (1971) revised the ASV more conservatively, and the New International Version (New Testament 1973, whole Bible 1978), produced by an international committee of evangelical scholars, became for decades the best-selling English Bible.

The following decades brought translations for nearly every tradition and purpose. Catholics produced the Jerusalem Bible (1966), the New American Bible (1970; revised edition 2011), and the New Jerusalem Bible (1985). The Jewish Publication Society produced a new Tanakh (completed 1985). The New King James Version (1982) modernized the KJV while keeping its textual basis. The New Revised Standard Version (1989) revised the RSV with inclusive language and became the standard in many universities and mainline churches, updated as the NRSVue in 2021. The New Living Translation (1996) turned Kenneth Taylor's paraphrase into a translation made from the original languages. The English Standard Version (2001) revised the RSV in a more literal and conservative direction. The Holman Christian Standard Bible (2004) became the Christian Standard Bible (2017). The NET Bible (2005) was published online with more than 60,000 translators' notes. The NASB was updated in 1995 and 2020, and the Legacy Standard Bible (2021) revised the NASB 1995.

The Berean Standard Bible, the English text used throughout this Study Bible, was first published in 2016 by the team behind the Bible Hub website under the name Berean Study Bible, and renamed Berean Standard Bible. On 30 April 2023 its text was placed in the public domain, so that anyone may print, quote, or build on it without permission. It aims at a middle register, close to the original but readable, and it is designed to be studied alongside the Hebrew and Greek, which is why this Study Bible can show the original word behind each English word and link it to its dictionary entry.

sections.body:
English Bibles use conventions that are rarely explained. The most important concerns the name of God. In the Old Testament, when you see LORD in capital and small capital letters, it stands for the Hebrew divine name YHWH, the personal name God revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:13-15), whose original pronunciation was probably Yahweh. Jewish reverence led readers to say Adonai, ‘Lord’, instead, and the Septuagint translated it with kyrios, ‘Lord’; English Bibles follow that tradition but mark the difference in type. When you see Lord in ordinary letters, it translates adonai or another word for master. So Psalm 110:1 reads “The LORD said to my Lord”, meaning ‘YHWH said to my master’, and Jesus builds an argument on those two words in Matthew 22:41-46. Where the Hebrew has Adonai YHWH together, English Bibles avoid ‘Lord LORD’ by writing Lord GOD, with GOD in small capitals, as in Abram's prayer, “O Lord GOD, what can You give me” (Genesis 15:2). A few translations, such as the Holman Christian Standard Bible and the Jerusalem Bible, print Yahweh in some or all places.

Italic type in the KJV, NKJV, and NASB marks words the translators supplied to make sense in English that have no direct equivalent in the original, such as a form of ‘to be’, which Hebrew and Greek often omit. It does not mean emphasis. Square brackets in many modern Bibles mark passages whose place in the original text is doubtful, most often the longer ending of Mark and the story of the woman caught in adultery (Mark 16:9-20, John 7:53-8:11). Footnotes carry several standard abbreviations: ‘Or’ introduces an alternative translation of the same words; ‘Heb.’ or ‘Gk.’ gives a literal rendering of the original; ‘Some manuscripts’ or ‘Other manuscripts’ introduces a textual variant; ‘MT’ is the Masoretic Text, ‘LXX’ the Septuagint, ‘DSS’ the Dead Sea Scrolls, ‘Syr.’ the Syriac, and ‘Vg.’ the Latin Vulgate.

Much of what is on the page is not in the original at all. Section headings (‘The Parable of the Sower’) are added by editors and are not part of the text. Chapter and verse numbers were added in the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries (see Chapters, Verses, and References). Punctuation, paragraphing, and quotation marks are editorial, since the original manuscripts had little or none, and deciding where a quotation ends can be an interpretation; in 1 Corinthians 7:1, for instance, most modern Bibles treat a sentence as a slogan quoted from the Corinthians' letter, while older ones read it as Paul's own statement. Poetry is set in indented lines because scholars recognize its parallel structure, though the manuscripts rarely lay it out that way. Red letters for the words of Jesus began with an edition of the New Testament published in 1899 by Louis Klopsch of The Christian Herald; they are a printer's aid, not a sign that other words are less inspired, and deciding where Jesus' words end (as in John 3) is itself an interpretation.

The best habit is to keep two translations open, one toward each end of the spectrum, and to read the footnotes. Where translations differ and footnotes appear, the reader has found a place where the original rewards a closer look.
